scope: Introductory development sanity checks; stories are three clusters, not 12 independent samples.
generation_author: Qwen/Qwen3-14B-AWQ if service available; no Codex model correction in primary scoring
story_author: Original retellings and controlled adaptations written by Codex as experiment author from familiar tales; no reproduced third-party passages.

budget.repair_policy: At most one targeted compiler-error repair for each controlled model. No gold, reference graph, expected answer or alignment enters repair.

analysis.primary: First attempts, failures in denominator; narrative source audit by Codex, independent researcher review pending.
analysis.controlled: Score four frozen interventions/story and full mapped behavior over all mapped-variable interventions when tractable; do not require identical identifiers.
analysis.natural: Preserve missing behavior; audit source support and test one frozen uncertainty question/story.
analysis.claims: Translate typed prose propositions to universal necessity, sufficiency, conjunction and inhibitory comparisons; enumerate all local rows and candidate functions. Conjunction requires necessity of EACH conjunct and joint sufficiency.
analysis.baseline: Three isolated direct-answer requests on same controlled text and four question wordings; no intermediate model/graph.
analysis.no_tuning: No reference changes after outputs, no prompt revisions to manufacture success; bounded technical repairs separately reported.

stories.title: Humpty Dumpty
stories.outcome: Humpty remains damaged after the repair attempt.

natural.text: Humpty Dumpty sat high on a wall, looking out over the road below.
He fell from the wall and lay damaged on the ground, unable to put himself back together.
The king sent his horses and his men, and the helpers gathered around Humpty to attempt a repair.
They worked at putting him together, but their efforts did not succeed, and Humpty remained damaged when they stopped.
The tale does not say what Humpty was made of, what techniques the helpers tried, or whether somebody else might have repaired him.
It describes this fall and this unsuccessful attempt, without settling what would happen with different equipment or a different kind of repair.

controlled.text: Humpty Dumpty sat on a wall, fell to the ground, and became damaged.
The king's helpers attempted a repair, but no effective repair method was available to them, and Humpty remained damaged.
Nothing here identifies Humpty as an egg or rules out a better repair elsewhere.
Added rule for this controlled adaptation: Humpty becomes damaged exactly when he falls; there are no other sources of initial damage in the model.
Added rule: a repair succeeds exactly when Humpty is damaged, the helpers attempt repair, and an effective method is available.
Added rule: Humpty remains damaged exactly when he became damaged and repair does not succeed.
Added background: falling, attempting repair, and method availability are independently settable inputs; mechanisms stay fixed when an input is changed.

reference.author: Codex, as experiment author; fixed scoring specification, not a discovered interpretation
background: No other initial damage; repair effectiveness is local to the specified helpers and attempt.

variables.label: Falls from the wall
variables.definition: 1 means Humpty falls in the episode; 0 means no fall.

variables.label: Damaged by the fall
variables.definition: 1 means Humpty has initial damage after the fall.

variables.label: Effective method available
variables.definition: 1 means an effective method is available to these helpers.

variables.label: Repair succeeds
variables.definition: 1 means the attempted repair removes the damage.

variables.label: Remains damaged
variables.definition: 1 means Humpty remains damaged after the attempt.

questions.text: If Humpty does not fall, does he remain damaged after the attempt?
If an effective method is available to the helpers, does Humpty remain damaged?
If an effective method is available but the helpers do not attempt repair, does Humpty remain damaged?
If the helpers do not attempt repair, with their factual lack of an effective method unchanged, does Humpty remain damaged?

natural_checks.question: Would an effective method available to the helpers guarantee that Humpty no longer remains damaged?
natural_checks.reason: A different repair is not described; availability alone does not establish its use or outcome.

stories.title: The Boy Who Cried Wolf
stories.outcome: The flock is harmed during the real wolf visit.

natural.text: A shepherd boy watching a flock near his village repeatedly shouted that a wolf was attacking when there was no wolf.
The villagers hurried out at these earlier alarms, found no danger, and grew unwilling to trust his warnings.
Later a real wolf appeared among the sheep, and the frightened boy shouted another warning.
The villagers took this new cry for another trick and did not come to help.
The wolf harmed the flock while the boy waited in vain for assistance.
This telling says nothing about the boy dying, how quickly help could have arrived, or whether every attack could have been stopped; it leaves those possibilities open.

controlled.text: A shepherd boy gave earlier false wolf alarms, and the villagers lost trust in him.
A real wolf then appeared, the boy gave a new warning, the villagers did not respond, and the flock was harmed.
Added rule for this controlled adaptation: villagers distrust the boy exactly when he has given earlier false alarms.
Added rule: the boy gives the new warning exactly when a real wolf appears, unless that warning is directly intervened on.
Added rule: villagers respond in time exactly when a new warning is given and they do not distrust the boy.
Added rule: the flock is harmed exactly when a real wolf appears and villagers do not respond in time; timely help always prevents harm in this adaptation.
Added background: earlier false alarms and the real wolf's appearance are separate inputs, and there are no other threats.

reference.author: Codex, as experiment author; fixed scoring specification, not a discovered interpretation
background: Timely response suffices to prevent harm; no other threats.

variables.label: Earlier false alarms
variables.definition: 1 means the boy has given earlier false alarms.

variables.label: Villagers distrust him
variables.definition: 1 means villagers distrust the new warning.

variables.label: Real wolf appears
variables.definition: 1 means a real wolf appears in the later episode.

variables.label: New warning given
variables.definition: 1 means the boy gives a new warning in the later episode.

variables.label: Villagers respond in time
variables.definition: 1 means villagers respond soon enough to prevent harm.

variables.label: Flock is harmed
variables.definition: 1 means the flock is harmed during the real wolf visit.

questions.text: If there had been no earlier false alarms, is the flock harmed during the later episode?
If no real wolf appears, is the flock harmed?
If there had been no earlier false alarms and the new warning is prevented, is the flock harmed?
If the new warning is prevented while the earlier false alarms remain as told, is the flock harmed?

natural_checks.question: If villagers had come to help, would the flock certainly have escaped harm?
natural_checks.reason: The natural telling does not establish response timing or guaranteed prevention.

stories.title: The Crow and the Pitcher
stories.outcome: The crow drinks from the pitcher.

natural.text: A thirsty crow found an intact pitcher holding some water, but the water was too low for its beak to reach.
Small stones lay nearby, and the crow began dropping them into the pitcher instead of abandoning the drink.
As stones collected inside, the water rose, and after enough stones had been added the crow could reach it.
The crow drank from the pitcher and relieved its thirst.
This telling describes the successful sequence without specifying how many stones were needed or what would happen if the pitcher leaked.
It also does not settle every alternative way the crow might have found a drink; its account is limited to this pitcher, these stones, and this attempt.

controlled.text: A thirsty crow found an intact pitcher containing sufficient water, initially below beak reach, with enough stones available nearby.
The crow added enough stones; the water rose, became reachable, and the crow drank.
Added rule for this controlled adaptation: the crow adds enough stones exactly when enough stones are available, unless that action is directly intervened on.
Added rule: water rises exactly when the pitcher is intact and enough stones are added.
Added rule: water is reachable exactly when the pitcher is intact and either water was initially within reach or it rises after stones are added.
Added rule: the crow drinks exactly when water is reachable.
Added background: sufficient water and the crow's readiness to drink stay fixed; pitcher integrity, stone availability, and initial reachability are separately settable inputs.

reference.author: Codex, as experiment author; fixed scoring specification, not a discovered interpretation
background: Sufficient water and willingness to drink fixed at 1; Boolean qualitative reachability, no numerical fluid model.

variables.label: Pitcher intact
variables.definition: 1 means the pitcher retains its water throughout the attempt.

variables.label: Enough stones available
variables.definition: 1 means enough stones are available nearby.

variables.label: Water initially reachable
variables.definition: 1 means water is initially within beak reach before adding stones.

variables.label: Enough stones added
variables.definition: 1 means the crow adds enough stones during the attempt.

variables.label: Water rises
variables.definition: 1 means water rises sufficiently during stone addition.

variables.label: Water now reachable
variables.definition: 1 means water is within beak reach after the attempt.

variables.label: Crow drinks
variables.definition: 1 means the crow drinks from this pitcher at the endpoint.

questions.text: If the crow does not add enough stones, does it drink from the pitcher?
If the pitcher is not intact, does the crow drink from it?
If the crow does not add enough stones but water is initially within reach, does it drink?
If water is initially within reach, with other inputs as told, does the crow drink?

natural_checks.question: If the pitcher were not intact, would the crow certainly fail to drink from it?
natural_checks.reason: The natural account explicitly leaves leakage behavior unspecified.
